2. The plaint case, in short, is that the plaintiff instituted title suit No. 111 of 1989 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Sripur, Magura for declaration of title and confirmation of possession. It is stated in the plaint that Lalit Mohan Chakrabarty was a owner of 1.13 acres of land appertaining to plots No. 1093/1250/1786 of khatian No. 1044 and Malancha Dasi got the same executing kabuliyat on 19-6-1946. Rent suit No. 1660 of 1952 was filed against Malancha for nonpayment of rent and the same was decreed. In execution of the said decree, the suit land was sold in auction. The father of the defendant Nos. 1-5 Kartik Chandra Biswas purchased the same in auction and got the possession through Court and annulled all the encumbrances by filing case No. 117 of 1953 under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Thereafter, one Shudanya alias Shudhansu filed Title suit No. 137 of 1956 for setting aside the aforesaid auction but the same was dismissed. Kartik Chandra Biswas the auction purchaser granted patta in favour of Belayet Ali Sheikh and Earuddin of 1.13 acres of land in 1362 B.S. i.e. 2-3-1956. 

 4. The defendant No.6 contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and stated inter alia that 8 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1093 out of 20 decimals, 5 decimals out of 32 decimals land of suit plot No. 1250, 10 decimals of land out of 60 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1786 and 7 decimals out of 44 decimals of non suit No. 116 and 7 decimals out of 41 decimals of land of non suit plot No. 117 belonged to Sudanya and, the father of the defendant No.6 purchased those lands by registered kabala dated 26-2-1953. 8 decimals of land out of plot No. 1093 acquired by WAPDA and the father of the defendant No.6 got compensation. The suit land has been correctly recorded in SA Khatian No. 1144. Kartik Chandra Biswas became owner by auction purchase in respect of 12 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1093 out of 21 decimals, 21 decimals out of 32 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1250 and 50 decimals out of 60 decimals of land of suit plot No. 1786 of the same was correctly recorded in SA Khatian No. 1143. Kartik Chandra Biswas sold land to Ataur Rahman by registered kabala deed 28-5-1969 and the father of the defendant No.6 being co- sharer filed preemption case in respect of the said kabala being Miscellaneous case No. 523 of 1970 which was allowed on contest. Said Ataur preferred Misc. Appeal No. 42 of 1975 and the said appeal was dismissed and preemption was confirmed. 

 9. The defendant No.6 again being dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court has preferred this revisional application before this Court and obtained the present Rule as stated above. 

 10. Mr. AH Mahfoozur Rahman learned Advocate along with Mr. Mashiul Alam, Advocate appearing. on behalf of the defendant No.6 petitioner has taken me through the judgment of both the Courts and placed the evidence of both the parties and submitted that the Trial Court on both facts and law committed error of law in passing the impugned judgment discarding the Rule of evidence. The evidence of DWs 2, 3 and 4 were also misread by the Courts below and further failed to note that the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title and confirmation and possession over only 52 and 1/2 decimals of land but the plaintiff produced PWs. 2 and 3 to corroborate the evidence of PW.l but PW.2 and 3 being the witness of possession only prove the possession of 16 decimals of land out of the 32 decimals of land of plot 1250 and without noticing, such evidence on record decreed the suit covering entire 52 and 1/2 decimals on surmises and, as such, the judgment of the Trial Court is not a judgment at all and that the Appellate Court without adverting to those materials on record affirmed the judgment of the Trial Court without having regard to the Order 41, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thereby, both the Courts committed error of law in decreeing the suit which is an error in the decision occasioning failure or justice. The learned Advocate submitted Kartik Chandra Biswas admittedly the auction purchaser allegedly granted patta in favour of plaintiff arid the proforma defendant No.11 Earuddin by alleged registered patta dated. 3-3-1956 but in fact, Kartik Chandra Biswas had no superior interest over the suit land at the relevant time, on tlie operation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act stated on 13-12- 1955 at the locality and, as such, the.alleged patta is a void document. He further submitted tlre plaintiff has filed the suit only for declaration of title and confirmation possession without partition, as according to the plaintiff got the patta along with the proforma defendant No. 11 and, as such, the suit itself is not maintainable but this vital aspect of the case lost sight of the Courts below and decreeing the suit committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He submitted further that the plaintiff only produced patta which has been marked as Exhibit 1 and no paper showing act of possession has been produced before the Court but the plaintiff has filed the suit and examined himself as PW 1 and 2 other witness PW 2 and 3 to support his possession, but those 2 witnesses only corroborated to the extent of 16 decimals of land and even such, materials on record the Courts below finding the title and possession of the plain- tiff oven the entire suit land had decreed the suit and thus committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 11. The learned Advocate further submitted that the father of the defendant No.6 he had not purchased the land from Kartik Chandra Biswas and he had no onus to prove the title of Kartik, but Kartik Chandra Biswas sold his land to one Ataur Rahman by registered kabala dated 28-5-1969 and the father of the defendant No.6 being co-sharer filed the pre-emption case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the preemption was confirmed up to Appellate Court, but said Ataur Rahman did not move the higher Court against the judgment, passed by the Appellate Court. The father of the defendant No. 6 got possession pursuant to the order of the Court passed in preemption case and in spite of such materials on record the Trial Court Shifted the onus to the defendant No.6 to prove the case as to title of Kartik which was not at all necessary because the father of the defendant No.6 only being preemptor got the land by pre-emption sold to Ataur Rahman by Kartik and in this score also the Trial Court as well as the Appellate Court have committed error of law in not noticing such evidence on record and decreeing the suit committed error of law resulting, in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate submitted further that the father of the defendant No.6 after receiving the judgment, and order of preemption case got mutated his name in SA Khatian No. 1144 and paid the rents and all the documents were made exhibits being exhibit No. Ka, Kha, Ga series Gha, Uma, Cha etc but those exhibits were not at all considered by the Trial Court as well as Appellate Court but decreed the suit which is liable to be set aside as committed error of law which has occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate has also submitted that the name of Kartik Chandra Biswas was recorded in SA Khatian which has been marked exhibit Uma(1) to show that Kartik had title and possession over the suit land who transferred his interest to Ataur Rahman and defendant father being co-sharer filed the pre-emption case and got the pre-emption but this aspect of the case was not taken into consideration by the Courts below and having passed the impugned judgment committed error of law which is an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 12. In support of his contention the learned Advocate has referred to the section 17 sub section 3 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act:- 

 "On the other hand, section 75 A, which was incorporated in 1954, came into operation only when a notification giving notice of the intention to undertake the preparation of the record of rights under section 17 (3) or of the compensation assessment roll under section 31 (1) had been given and it placed a complete embargo only on the subletting of any land in the khas possession of any rent-receiver within the area or areas specified in the notification and subletting, if made in contravention of the said section, was made null and void. The land so sublet was also to stand forfeited to the Provincial Government after the amendments made to the said section in 1956. The intention of this section appears to be that since after the acquisition of the interests of rent-receivers, rent-receivers were themselves to retain certain classes of retainable Khas lands as tenants directly under the Government, they should not be allowed to create further sub-tenancies under them. This was in keeping with the scheme of the acquisition Act, which was that after the acquisition of all rent-receiving interest anyone who held land within the province of East Pakistan should hold it as a tenant or raiyat directly under the government and not under anyone else as an intermediary. 

 'Sub-letting' has, of course, not been defined under the Act but under section 2 (31) of the Act words used in the first IV Parts of the Act (within which section 75A occurs) and not defined therein are to be given the same meaning as they bear in the Bengal Tenancy Act. Or Sylhet tenancy Act "Subletting" under the latter Acts connotes the creation of a subordinate tenancy or under raiyati under which the sub-lessee would but for a special contract be liable to pay rent for that land to a person other than the Provincial Government. Section 75A was intended to prevent this eventuality and this intention is made further manifest by the provisions of sub-section (3) thereof which provide that if any person holding land in his Khas possession does not wish to retain the same in his khas he may apply to the Provincial Government for the acquisition thereof on payment of compensation at the prescribed rate." 

 13. The learned Advocate then refers to section 75A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and submitted that the alleged patta having been made in contravention of the sub section I of section 75A shall be null and void section 75A runs as follows: 

 (3) Any person may, at any time, apply to the Government for the acquisition of any of his khas lands under sub-section (2) of section 3 on payment of compensation at the rate prescribed for such land in section 39." 

 "10. It appears from the impugned judgment that although the learned Judges have stated that the Courts below based their judgments upon misreading and non-consideration of the evidence, yet they failed to lay their hands on any part of the evidence of PWs and DWs or on any documentary evidence to bring home this error of law on the part of the Courts below. Without reversing the findings of the Courts below on the grounds mentioned in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure the High Court Division has no-jurisdiction to disturb the final findings of facts. It cannot superimpose itself as a third Court for fresh appreciation of evidence. That is not its function in the revisional jurisdiction." 

 "8. The rent-receipts were excluded from consideration by the lower Appellate Court taking the view that these are provisional receipts and that they carry little weight in that "any person interested in a land may pay rent to the Government Acquired Estate." This view is erroneous, for rent-receipts, though no documents of title are important items of evidence of possession any may be used as collateral evidence of title since possession generally follows title. Again plaintiff's name has also been recorded in the SA Khatian prepared in the period immediately following the whole-sale state acquisition in 1956 and all objections raised by defendant No. 1 were overruled by the Revenue-officer and then by the appellate authority. " 

 "Nevertheless, the lessee continued in possession with the consent of the landlords who realized rent from him after the expiry of the period of one year and in this way be continued till the Whole sale State Acquisition when he became a tenant directly under the Government. It is the possession of the lessee which is of fundamental importance in the case of holding over."

 25. Upon analyses of the aforesaid evidence, pleading of the plaint along with the prayer and schedule and findings of the Trial Court, it appears that the Trial Court failed to notice that the plaintiff only submitted the patta deed 3-3-1956, exhibit-I and no papers showing his subsequent mode of possession has been produced before the Court. During the cross examination the PW 1 clearly stated that :“আমি নালিশী জমির খাজনা দেই না” and the name of the Kartik is still appearing in the khatians and such evidence clearly indicated that after the alleged patta the plaintiff did not take any step to record his land in the subsequent record of rights and admittedly, the plaintiff is not paying rent to the Government and no document had been produced .to show his possession in any manner in the suit land and the PW 2 and 3 only proved possession over 16 decimals of land out of 32 decimals of land in respect of plot No. 1250 but the plaintiff filed the suit for 52 and 1/2 decimals of land and thereby, it is clear that the plaintiff could not prove his title over the entire suit land as the PW 2 and 3 only allegedly corroborated to the extent of 16 decimals of plot No. 1250. 

 27. Now let me deal with the legal aspect of the case. The defendant petitioner acquired the title through preemption case as a co-sharer of the case land which was sold by Kartik to Ataur Rahman. It appears in the pleadings of the parties that Kartik admittedly acquired the land from Shudhamay and got the possession through Court and annulled all the encumbrances by filing case No. 117 of 1953 under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Against the auction sale one Shudhanshu filed Suit No. 137 of 1956 for setting aside the aforesaid auction sale and the suit was dismissed and the sale was confirmed. Both the parties claim title through Kartik. The plaintiff allegedly took patta from Kartik on 3-3-1956 but thereafter, the plaintiff did not take any step to record his name in the relevant Khatian or mutated his name in the record and also admittedly has not paid rent to any authority, what so ever, since 1956. It is evident on record that the plaintiff has failed to show any papers showing possession except the patta and oral evidence of PW 1, 2 and 3. PWs 2 and 3 only allegedly proved possession over 16 decimals of land though the suit is for 52-1/2 decimals land. On the other hand the defendant claimed that after December 1955 the Kartik had no authority to grant patta holding rent receiving interest as rent receiving interest had already been ceased in view of publication of notification dated 13-12-1955 under sub-section 3 of section 17 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The defendant submitted that Kartik did not execute such patta as he had no superior interest. The plaintiff also did not take step to examine the signature of the Kartik in order to prove the patta. It has already been submitted that Kartik being owner recorded his name in the SA Khatians and being in possession sold land out of 3 plots vide exhibit-C to one Ataur Rahman and the father of the defendant No. 6 being co-sharer filed preemption case and got the preemption up to Appellate Court, but the plaintiff did never take any step to dislodge those SA Khatians as well as the sale deed executed by Kartik and so also the pre-emption case but remained silent. It appears further the defendant No. 11 who is the co-recipient of patta dated 3-3-1956 along with the plaintiff filed suit No. 115 of 1977 in the Court of Assistant Judge Magura and the defendant ultimately won the case in the Appellate stage contesting Title Appeal No. 485 of 1983 and on the face of such material evidence on record, the plaintiff did not take any step what so ever and such silence on the part of the plaintiff clearly proved that he failed to prove his patta deed and possession. It is on record that the defendant did not purchase land from Kartik but got the land of exhibit-'C' by preemption and, as such, from the evidence on record the defendant was not supposed to know about the basis of the acquisition of land by Kartik and, as such, defend in not bound to prove as to the acquisition of title by Kartik and in spite of such materials on record, Trial Court shifted the onus of proof upon the defendant and giving finding as such, it appears that the Courts below committed error of law. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party has tried to establish title on the basis of patta but no cogent evidence has been adduced before the Court. The learned Advocate has relied upon several decisions as noted above to get the decree on the basis of the decisions inasmuch as on the basis of holding over, adverse possession and as well as findings of the Courts below as the Courts below, concurrently settled the facts in favour of the plaintiff but the decisions cited by the learned Advocate are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case.
